title: MEA Blames Patrol Deviations as India, China Agree LAC Talks
excerpt: Responding to the ITBP chief's disclosure of continuing Arunachal face-offs, the foreign ministry said both sides will discuss improving understanding of the LAC for better border management.
body:
• India's foreign ministry said on Friday the border situation is disturbed when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns, responding to the ITBP chief's disclosure of continuing face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh.
  • MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said both sides continue to use diplomatic and military mechanisms and have agreed to discuss ways to improve understanding of the LAC for better border management.
  • Opposition leaders including Congress and AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi demanded greater transparency, with Owaisi calling for an independent report and a special session of Parliament.
  • The exchange revives scrutiny of the post-2020 border framework, two years after the October 2024 patrolling agreement restored access at Depsang and Demchok in eastern Ladakh.

India's Ministry of External Affairs said on Friday that the situation along the border with China is disturbed when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns, in its first public response to the border police chief's disclosure that face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh have occurred in recent days and are continuing.

MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, asked about remarks by Indo-Tibetan Border Police Director General Shatrujeet Singh Kapur, referred questions on specifics to the Ministry of Defence but restated New Delhi's long-standing position. "As we have noted in the past, the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns," Jaiswal said at the regular media briefing.

"The maintenance of peace and tranquillity in the border areas is essential for the overall development of bilateral relations."

— Randhir Jaiswal, MEA spokesperson

What the MEA added

Jaiswal said both sides "continue to use existing diplomatic and military mechanisms to resolve outstanding issues and avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation along the Line of Actual Control." He added that the two sides have also agreed to discuss ways to improve understanding of the LAC in appropriate areas for better border management — the newest element in Friday's statement, suggesting the Arunachal friction will be taken up through the existing consultation channels rather than treated as a closed episode.

Kapur, speaking at the Himveer Samman Samaroh ceremony in Alwar, Rajasthan, had said: "In the past few days, a situation arose where face-offs happened at several locations in Arunachal and it still continues." He praised the newly raised Shaurya Commandos for their performance during the confrontations and said the ITBP is strengthening drone and anti-drone capabilities and building underground shelters along the border, describing the China front as India's "most difficult" border.

Opposition demands answers

The disclosure drew sharp opposition reactions. Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge called the ITBP chief's confirmation deeply alarming and urged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to come clean on the border situation, according to coverage of the party's response. Congress communications chief Jairam Ramesh criticised the government for remaining silent on the face-offs, cited reports of corps commander-level talks following a face-off at Taksing, and pointed to India's trade deficit with China, which he said reached a record $112 billion in 2025-26.

AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi demanded a comprehensive, independent report and said a special session of Parliament should be convened to discuss the situation and the government's China policy. In a post on X reported by IANS, Owaisi sought "a complete clarification on the number of places in Arunachal where the Chinese troops have intruded, stopped our patrols and citizens and are refusing to leave," and asked how long the situation had continued. No response from Beijing to Friday's MEA remarks was carried in the reports reviewed for this article.

Why the patrolling pattern matters

The LAC, roughly 3,488 km long, is not a mutually agreed boundary, and differing perceptions of where it runs have produced localised face-offs for decades. The current framework dates to the crisis that followed the June 2020 Galwan Valley clash, in which 20 Indian soldiers were killed. After years of corps commander talks, India and China reached an agreement on 21 October 2024 on patrolling arrangements that completed disengagement in eastern Ladakh, restoring patrolling at Depsang and Demchok, and Prime Minister Modi and President Xi Jinping met days later in Kazan to restart broader engagement.

Friday's exchange tests that framework in the eastern sector, where China claims Arunachal Pradesh in its entirety — a claim India rejects. The MEA's formulation places the onus for disturbances on deviations from agreed patrolling patterns while keeping the diplomatic door open. What to watch is whether the promised discussion on improving LAC understanding produces a concrete outcome, and whether the Defence Ministry provides the specifics Jaiswal deferred.
